reason: Paragraph opens flatly: 'The production of the lapis was the goal of alchemy in general' (§759). Direction and quote exact; Dorn is noted as an exception, but the edge claims the general goal, which is what Jung asserts.

The paragraph says Dorn's third degree of conjunction was 'the union of the whole man with the unus mundus'; the self is named only as the analogous ground of personality and as the basis ('On the basis of a self... Dorn hoped') from which the union proceeds — the self is not the party united.

'This potential world is the "mundus archetypus" of the Schoolmen' (§761), where 'this potential world' is the unus mundus of §760. Designation correctly attributed to the Schoolmen as jung-reports-parallel.

'there can be no doubt about its tendency to spiritualize the "body"' (§763), 'its' referring to the opus alchymicum. 'No doubt' makes this a firm assertion of the tendency; the mutual counter-movement (concretizing spirit) is captured separately in edge 5.

'In reality his labours elevated the body into proximity with the spirit while at the same time drawing the spirit down into matter. By sublimating matter he concretized spirit' (§764) — the alchemist's opus concretizes spirit; direction and quote correct.

The paragraph frames this as the alchemist's belief ('the alchemist thought he knew... the anima mundi entered into material things and was caught there'), so jung-reports-parallel is the right claim_type and direction (anima mundi caught in matter) is correct.

'Dorn's caelum, which corresponded to the stone... For the psychologist it is the self' (§765) — Jung himself makes the psychological identification, so jung-asserts with relation symbolizes is right.

The 'air-coloured liquid' (the caelum/quintessence) 'represents nothing less than a corpus glorificationis, the resurrected body' (§763). The parallel to the Christian resurrected body is a reported theological designation, correctly jung-reports-parallel.

The paragraph says Christ is 'a dividing "sword" which sunders the spiritual man from the physical' (§773) — a separation between spiritual man and physical man, not an action done to 'the body' as sole object. The object misstates what is sundered.

The text is conditional and its subject is doctrinal, not Christ himself: 'In that case the Christian standpoint would correspond to the unio mentalis in the overcoming of the body' (§773). A hedged claim about the Christian standpoint has been flattened into an assertion about Christ as symbol.

'the experience of the self is always a defeat for the ego' (§778) is a flat, unhedged assertion with correct direction (self overpowering ego, prototyped by Job and Yahweh); Jung's later caveat concerns whether the ego deserves defeat, not whether the experience constitutes one.

Mandala symbolism 'portrays the self as a concentric structure, often in the form of a squaring of the circle' (§776) — the squaring of the circle is a symbolic form portraying the self; direction correct.

The paragraph describes the active-imagination procedure (entering the fantasy drama with personal reactions) and concludes 'This is where insight, the unio mentalis, begins to become real' (§753) — the process is what makes the unio mentalis real; direction correct.

The one who 'risked the fight with the dragon and is not overcome by it' — the hero — 'attained what the alchemists called the unio mentalis' (§756). Quote exact; the alchemical term is attributed but the attainment claim is Jung's own.

'the integration of the unconscious with consciousness, whereby both are altered' (§779): the unconscious is what is integrated into consciousness, matching the edge direction; the mutual alteration does not reverse it.

'when we talk of God or gods we are speaking of debatable images from the psychoid realm' (§787) — the God-image (not God) comes from the psychoid realm; the edge correctly targets the image, and the 'realization might be dawning' framing is rhetorical, not a genuine hedge.
The opus 'was a work of reconciliation between apparently incompatible opposites', understood as both physical and moral conflict (§790). Direction and quote correct.
